title.text: Data readiness assessment, roadmap and 90-day plan (practical)

objects.text: How ready is my organisation’s data for AI, what will I fix first, and who will own it?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 14 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome to the last session. Over thirteen sessions you have seen how models learn, how language models work, how to prompt and check them, what agents can do, and how to set rules and question vendors. Today the question turns to your own organisation. Is the information ready for any of this, what do you fix first, and who owns it? You leave with a plan, three dates and the follow-up kit.

Here is what you leave with. An inventory of your information and a readiness scorecard scored out of twelve. A roadmap and a ninety day plan, where every action has an owner, a date, the hours and a measure that someone else can check. The follow-up kit for the check-ins.

And one picture of all fourteen sessions, which you can explain to a colleague in a minute. Nobody scores you. The plan is the result.

title.text: Your last two hours: 55 minutes build your plan

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_2a1ea620.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: 55 of the 120 minutes are yours: inventory, scorecard, roadmap, check-ins.

slides.notes:
This is the last session, so it builds the plan you take back to work. After a short recall of Session 13, I explain the five kinds of data, the readiness scorecard and the six steps from scattered records to AI-ready data. Then I count what is wrong in the NVF files.

After the break you build your inventory, your scorecard, your roadmap and your check-ins. We finish with one decision and a look back over all fourteen sessions.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  How is a risk scored in the Risk Register, and which scores are High?
2.  Name two red flags in the OrbitDesk proposal and the question each one needs.
3.  My understanding: which law covers personal data in AI tools in Uganda, and who confirms it for you?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 13. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. How is a risk scored in the Risk Register, and which scores are High? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Likelihood from 1 to 5 times impact from 1 to 5. High is 15 or more, Medium is 8 to 14, Low is below 8.

Question two. Name two red flags in the OrbitDesk proposal and the question each one needs. Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Any two of: payments with no approval step, a request for bank login, training on your data by default, 36 months with no exit, no usage cap, no references, a deadline. For each, ask for the control, the proof or the clause in writing.

Question three. My understanding: which law covers personal data in AI tools in Uganda, and who confirms it for you? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. The Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019. Your lawyer confirms which duties apply to your uses.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Data readiness. How far your information is readable, findable, complete and allowed to be used with AI.

Inventory. A written list of what information you hold, who owns it, where it lives and who may see it.

Metadata. Facts about a file, such as date, owner and version, that help you find and trust it.

Roadmap. A plan of actions, each with an owner, dates, hours and a way to check it worked.

Check-in. A short review at day 30, 60 and 90 of your plan, with a test and a decision.

title.text: Five kinds of data, five first steps

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t14_fivekinds_11.90x4.25_629227f2.png
objects.alt: Five kinds of data, five first steps

objects.text: Tables are structured. The rest is unstructured.

slides.notes:
You met these five kinds of data in Session 0, and the technical sessions showed why each matters. Session 1 showed that an image is a grid of numbers, and a scan is only a picture until text is read from it. Session 4 showed that text becomes numbers called embeddings.

For each kind there is one first step. Define every column in a table. Find the current version of a text. Read the words out of an image and check a sample. Transcribe sound and remove phone numbers. Check sensor readings for gaps. Which kind does your organisation hold most of?

objects.text: Amber means usable after a named fix. Points: Green 2, Amber 1, Red 0, so a total out of 12.

slides.notes:
This is the readiness scorecard from the Information Inventory template. Six areas, each with a rule you can apply. Inventory: is there a written list with owners?

Readable: can the text be selected and copied?

Complete and unique: one current copy, with no gaps?

Metadata: date, owner and version on each file?

Rights: is it written down who may use it?

Current: updated on a schedule?

Green scores two points, Amber one, Red zero, so the total is out of twelve. A Red on rights stops the project until a lawyer has looked. Where will your first Red be?

slides.notes:
This is a recorded run on 6 November 2026, with a short Python script. No AI model is used. I open the three NVF practice files and count. The invoice file has sixty rows and eight faults: four wrong totals, two missing purchase order numbers, one line with zero VAT and one duplicate.

The customer messages file has forty rows, and thirty two sender cells hold a phone number, which is personal data. The sales file has three hundred and sixty rows and no definition of revenue. The script is in the demonstration folder, so you can run it on your own files.

title.text: Six steps turn scattered files into AI-ready data

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_28fe3d24.png
objects.alt: Six steps turn scattered files into AI-ready data

objects.text: Start with one folder and one task. Test it, then widen.

slides.notes:
Six steps take scattered records to AI-ready data. One, inventory: list every source, its owner and its format. Two, digitise: scan paper and read the text with optical character recognition. Three, clean: remove duplicates and fix errors. Four, describe: add date, owner and version, or for legal files the court and citation.

Five, protect: set who can see what and mask personal data. Six, index and test: cut the text into chunks, turn them into embeddings, and ask real questions with known answers. Skipping the last step is the usual mistake. Start with one folder and one task.

title.text:
A scan is a picture until text is read
from it, and labels make it findable

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t14_docjourney_7.70x4.80_f35cdad5.png
objects.alt: A scan is a picture until text is read from it, and labels make it findable

objects.text: Each stage changes what a model can do with the page.

runs.text: Session 4: text becomes numbers called embeddings.
Session 9: retrieval finds the closest passages.

slides.notes:
Follow one page through the stages. On paper, a model can do nothing with it. A scan is a picture, a grid of numbers as in Session 1, so still no words. After optical character recognition there is text, though it may have errors, so you check a sample.

Cut into chunks with labels such as date and owner, the page is ready for the retrieval you saw in Session 9. Turned into embeddings and indexed, as in Session 4, it can be found by meaning. Preparing data for search is lighter than preparing it for training. Start with search.

title.text:
The first test is twenty
questions with known answers

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_3f479fe8.png
objects.alt: The first test is twenty questions with known answers

objects.text: Write the line for success first. About 50 questions give a firmer result.

slides.notes:
In Session 10 you scored a ten question test set. The same idea tests your data. Pick twenty real questions that staff ask. Write the correct answer and the source file for each. Add two or three traps that the files cannot answer, because the right reply is that the files do not say.

Run the questions with your files attached. Score each answer as right, wrong or invented, and fix the gaps. Write the line for success before you run it, for example sixteen of twenty right and none invented. Fifty questions give a firmer result.

title.text:
Worked example: rights and
cleaning come before the test

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_roadmap_11.90x4.25_028537ac.png
objects.alt: Worked example: rights and cleaning come before the test

objects.text: NVF plan, 1 February 2027. Red arrows show what waits.

slides.notes:
Here is the data roadmap for Nile Valley Foods, drawn from the 90-Day Roadmap template. The plan starts on the first of February. The gold bar is the retrieval test, and it waits for three things: the invoice file fixed, the data dictionary written and the phone numbers masked.

Masking waits for the data sharing rule, because rights is the Red area. The red arrows show these dependencies. Order matters. If you test before you fix rights, you test something you may not be allowed to use. Each bar has one named owner. Who would own the first bar in your roadmap?

These are the six lines behind the picture, using the real columns of the Roadmap sheet: action, owner, due date, effort in hours, depends on, and success measure. A success measure is a number that someone else can check. Better data quality is a wish. Zero faults on recheck by the nineteenth of February is a measure.

Sixteen of twenty test questions right, with none invented, is a measure. The hours are estimates, and the whole plan is about thirty five hours across five people. Which of your own actions needs a measure like these?

title.text:
Three check-ins keep the plan
honest: day 30, day 60 and day 90

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t14_checkins_11.90x4.25_974eec7f.png
objects.alt: Three check-ins keep the plan honest: day 30, day 60 and day 90

slides.notes:
After this session your plan runs for ninety days from the start date you choose. The dates on the slide are for NVF, starting on the first of February. At day thirty you bring the Check-in Form and your roadmap, and the test is whether your policy controls are in place and your first gap is closed.

At day sixty you add a row from the Results Tracker, and the test is whether any stop rule is met and whether actions are on time. At day ninety you bring the Sponsor Briefing and re-score the six areas. Then you decide: continue, expand, pause or stop. Your lecturer messages you before each date.

title.text:
Practice: list your sources
and label each by sensitivity

objects.text: 15 minutes
Hands-on, on your own organisation
Build your Information Inventory.

runs.text: Open Information Inventory.xlsx, sheet Inventory. Start from row 7.
One source per row: Source, Owner, Format, Where it lives, Who may see it.
Mark Sensitivity: Public, Internal or Confidential, plus Personal for a living person.
Mark Ready for AI: Yes, Fix first or No, and What to fix first.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_5683a888.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: An inventory of at least six sources, each labelled and owned.

slides.notes:
Open the Information Inventory and use the Inventory sheet from row seven. The three grey rows show NVF examples. List every source your organisation holds that an AI tool might touch, one per row. Write the owner, the format, where it lives and who may see it. Then label it public, internal or confidential, and add personal when it identifies a living person.

Finally mark whether it is ready for AI: yes, fix first, or no. Include the awkward sources, such as WhatsApp orders and files on personal phones. Aim for at least six rows.

Then pick your top three gaps, the Red or Amber areas that block your work most, and for each write the evidence, a first fix and a possible owner. Tell me your total and your first Red.

Open the 90-Day Roadmap, sheet Roadmap. First write your plan start date, and the check-in dates follow. Then write one action for each of your gaps. Each line needs a phase, an action a person can finish, one owner, a start, a due date and the effort in hours.

The three phases are protect and clean, describe and prepare, and test and decide. Fill Depends on so that rights and cleaning come before any test. Then rewrite each success measure as a number someone else can check. Aim for six actions. Finish the rest after class.

Three more sheets in the same workbook. On Check-ins, read the three dates that follow from your start date and put them in your diary now. On Decisions, write each decision your organisation must make during the ninety days, who decides, and by when. For NVF one is approving the data sharing rule.

On Risks, list three risks to the plan itself, including at least one about people being away, such as the owner of a key action. Write what you will do about each. Finally name the person you will tell first about this plan.

Decision: how much will you
take on in the next 90 days?

Test one folder now. Only if rights are not Red.
Say your choice aloud and write it at the top of your roadmap.

slides.notes:
One decision before we look back. How much will you take on in the next ninety days?

One gap, finished, gives you a real measured result at day ninety, and it is what I recommend for most. Three gaps, started, gives more to talk about and less certainty. Prove retrieval first suits you only if rights is not Red, because testing data you may not use is the wrong order.

Say your choice aloud, and write it at the top of your roadmap. Then name one action you will take in the next twenty four hours.

title.text:
Fourteen sessions are one picture:
from pixels to your 90-day plan

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t14_course_11.90x4.25_4e09745d.png
objects.alt: Fourteen sessions are one picture: from pixels to your 90-day plan

objects.text: Session 0 asked: what do I need to understand about AI before I decide anything about it?

slides.notes:
Here is the whole course in one picture. The top row is how models work: pixels and neurons, learning from examples, measuring a model, words as numbers, language models and foundation models. The middle row is how you use, shape and check them: open weights and file sizes, prompting, giving a model your knowledge, when models fail, and agents.

The bottom row is what you did with your own organisation: you mapped a workflow, wrote rules and questions for vendors, and built a data plan. Pick one station that changed how you think. Then answer the question we began the course with, in two sentences: what do you now understand about AI before you decide anything about it?

title.text:
What you now hold: your working
papers and your follow-up kit

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t14_shelf_11.90x4.25_0eecf37c.png
objects.alt: What you now hold: your working papers and your follow-up kit

slides.notes:
This is everything you now hold. Working papers for choosing and measuring a task, for briefing and checking a model, for building and limiting an automation, for governing and buying, and for your data and your plan. In gold is the follow-up kit: the Check-in Form, the Results Tracker and the Sponsor Briefing.

The templates carry some older session numbers, so go by the file names. Papers do nothing alone. The plan works when each action has a named owner and each date is in a diary. In the next twenty four hours, book the dates and tell each owner their action.
